title: Academic Writing Grammar
description: Master academic writing grammar for Grade 12: hedging language, impersonal constructions, citation reporting verbs, cause-effect and comparison language — bilingual notes, practice and tests.

topics.title: Hedging & Impersonal Constructions
topics.concept:
Hedging softens a claim so it is defensible — academics rarely state things as absolute fact:

  • Modals: may, might, could, would — 'This may indicate…'
  • Verbs: seem, appear, tend to, suggest — 'It appears that…', 'Prices tend to rise.'
  • Adverbs/phrases: possibly, perhaps, arguably, to some extent, it is likely that.

Impersonal constructions remove 'I/you' to sound objective:

  • Passive: It was observed that…, The data were analysed…
  • 'It'-structures: It is argued that…, It is widely believed that…, It should be noted that…
  • 'There'-structures: There is evidence to suggest that…

Together, hedging and impersonality create the careful, neutral voice of scholarship.

examples.problem: Rewrite impersonally: I found that the results were inconsistent.
examples.solution: It was found that the results were inconsistent.

recap: Hedge with modals (may/might), verbs (seem/tend to/suggest), adverbs (possibly)
Use impersonal 'It is argued that…', passive, and 'There is evidence that…'
Together they create a cautious, objective academic voice

topics.title: Citation Verbs, Cause-Effect & Comparison Language
topics.concept:
Reporting (citation) verbs let you present sources precisely, each implying a stance:

  • Neutral: states, notes, observes, describes.
  • Argument: argues, claims, maintains, contends, proposes.
  • Evidence: demonstrates, shows, reveals, indicates.
  • Disagreement: refutes, challenges, disputes, questions.

e.g. Sharma (2020) argues that… / The study demonstrates that…

Cause-effect language: leads to, results in, gives rise to, contributes to, is attributed to, stems from, owing to, as a consequence.

Comparison/contrast language: similarly, likewise, in contrast, whereas, while, compared to, in comparison with, conversely, on the other hand.

These phrases are the connective tissue of an academic argument.

examples.problem: Choose a cause-effect phrase: Deforestation ___ soil erosion.
examples.solution: leads to / results in / gives rise to soil erosion.

examples.problem: Choose a citation verb (showing evidence): The experiment ___ a clear link.

recap: Citation verbs carry a stance: argues, demonstrates, refutes, notes
Cause-effect: leads to, results in, stems from, is attributed to
Comparison: similarly, in contrast, whereas, compared to

questions.q: Choose the most appropriately hedged claim.
options: Social media may contribute to a decline in attention spans.
Everyone knows social media is terrible.

questions.q: Which citation verb implies the writer's disagreement with a source?
Rewrite impersonally and cautiously: 'I'm sure the policy worked.'
options: The policy appears to have been effective.
I personally know the policy worked.

questions.q: Choose the correct cause-effect structure: 'The decline ___ several interrelated factors.'
Which sentence best balances claim and caution?
options: The results prove the hypothesis beyond doubt.
The results lend some support to the hypothesis, though further study is needed.
The results say the hypothesis is right.

questions.q: Choose the precise comparison phrase: 'Group A improved markedly; ___, Group B showed no change.'
Identify the over-claim that needs hedging: 'This single study confirms that the drug cures the disease.'
options: confirms … cures → suggests … may help treat
questions.explanation: A single study cannot 'confirm a cure'; hedge it.

questions.q: Which reporting structure correctly cites a source's argument?
options: Mehta (2022) argues that the reform was premature.
Mehta (2022) argue that the reform was premature.
Mehta (2022), the reform was premature argues.
questions.explanation: 'Author (year) argues that …' is the standard citation pattern.

outcomes: Use hedging language to make cautious claims
Write with impersonal and passive constructions
Use precise reporting verbs for citing sources

intro.en: Academic English has its own grammar of caution and objectivity. Instead of 'I think it's true', a scholar writes 'The evidence suggests that this may be the case.' This chapter teaches the four pillars of that style — hedging, impersonality, citation verbs, and cause-effect/comparison language — so your essays and reports read like genuine academic work.
intro.hi: शैक्षणिक अंग्रेज़ी का अपना सतर्कता और वस्तुनिष्ठता का व्याकरण है। 'I think it's true' के बजाय विद्वान लिखता है 'The evidence suggests that this may be the case।' यह अध्याय उस शैली के चार स्तंभ सिखाता है — hedging, impersonality, citation verbs, और cause-effect/comparison language — ताकि आपके निबंध और रिपोर्ट सच्चे शैक्षणिक कार्य की तरह पढ़ें।

real_life.situation:
From a casual claim to an academic one:

Casual: Junk food makes kids fat.
Academic: It has been found that the regular consumption of processed food may contribute to obesity in children.
real_life.why: The academic version hedges ('may contribute'), is impersonal ('It has been found'), and is precise ('regular consumption of processed food'). This cautious, objective grammar is exactly what examiners and academic readers expect.

quick_test.q: Which phrase is an example of hedging?
quick_test.explanation: 'may suggest' softens the claim — that is hedging.

common_mistakes.wrong: I think pollution is bad and everyone knows it.
common_mistakes.right: It is widely held that pollution poses a serious threat.
common_mistakes.note: Avoid personal/absolute claims; hedge and use impersonal forms.
Academic writing rarely claims absolute proof.

common_mistakes.wrong: The study tells that prices rose.
common_mistakes.right: The study shows / indicates that prices rose.

common_mistakes.wrong: Pollution makes diseases because of it.

items.answer: It was found that the test was effective.
The consumption of junk food may adversely affect health.

error_detection.sentence: This proves 100% that it is true.
error_detection.correct: This strongly suggests that it is true.

error_detection.sentence: I personally feel the data is good.
error_detection.correct: The data appear to be reliable.

error_detection.sentence: The report tells that sales fell.
error_detection.correct: The report indicates that sales fell.

error_detection.sentence: Pollution makes diseases due to it.

sentence_correction.wrong: Everyone knows climate change is real.
sentence_correction.correct: It is widely accepted that climate change is real.

sentence_correction.wrong: The study tells the medicine works.
sentence_correction.correct: The study demonstrates that the medicine is effective.

sentence_correction.wrong: Stress gives heart problems because of it.
sentence_correction.correct: Stress may contribute to heart problems.

rearrangement.jumbled: that / it / argued / is / failed / the / policy
rearrangement.answer: It is argued that the policy failed.

reading.passage: It has been observed that urban air quality tends to deteriorate during winter. Several studies suggest that this may be attributed to a combination of traffic emissions and weather patterns. Sharma (2021) argues that vehicle restrictions could significantly reduce pollution, whereas other researchers contend that the effect would be limited. The evidence, on the whole, indicates that a single measure is unlikely to solve the problem.

questions.q: Identify two hedging expressions and explain their purpose.
questions.answer: 'tends to', 'may be attributed to', 'could', 'is unlikely to' — they make the claims cautious and defensible.
